definition: The bandwidth some OSPF implementations divide by an interface's bandwidth to get its cost. Classic Cisco IOS uses 100 Mbit/s, so every link of 100 Mbit/s or faster costs 1 unless it is raised.
example: Raising the reference to 100 Gbit/s makes a 10 Gbit/s routing link cost 10.

definition: A group of OSPF routers and links that share one link-state database. Splitting a network into areas limits flooding and SPF work.
example: A campus might put each building in its own area, all attached to area 0.

definition: The OSPF backbone area used for ordinary inter-area routing. Other areas need suitable backbone connectivity, which can include configured virtual links; it is a routing architecture rule rather than a claim that every possible packet trace crosses a physical area-zero link.
example: Area border routers connect areas 1 and 2 to area 0.

definition: Area border router: an OSPF router attached to multiple areas that calculates and advertises inter-area reachability. A summary LSA can describe one prefix; aggregating several prefixes requires the relevant configuration.
example: An ABR in areas 0 and 3 tells area 0 which prefixes area 3 contains.

definition: Autonomous system boundary router: an OSPF router that injects routes learnt from outside OSPF, such as a default route or BGP routes.
example: The Internet-edge router acts as an ASBR, advertising a default route into OSPF.

definition: An OSPF configuration that connects an area to the backbone logically through another area, when it has no direct attachment to area 0.
example: Area 5 reaches area 0 by a virtual link through area 4.

definition: An OSPF route to a destination in a different area, learnt from summary information sent by an area border router rather than from that area's full topology.
example: A router in area 1 learns 10.3.0.0/16 in area 3 as an inter-area route with a cost from its ABR.

definition: On a shared segment such as an Ethernet LAN, the OSPF router elected to form adjacencies with all others and describe the segment in one LSA. Routers that are neither DR nor BDR are DROthers.
example: With 10 routers on a LAN, a DR and BDR cut adjacencies from 45 to 17.

definition: Backup designated router: the OSPF router that also forms adjacencies with everyone on a shared segment and takes over if the DR fails.
example: An existing BDR can take over the DR role with already established adjacencies; remaining protocol work and failure detection still take time.

definition: A 32-bit number, written like an IPv4 address, uniquely identifying a router in OSPF or BGP. It breaks ties in DR election and some BGP decisions.
example: A router with ID 10.255.0.1 is often numbered after its loopback address.

definition: An OSPF interface setting (0–255) used in DR election; higher wins and 0 means the router is never elected DR or BDR. Operators set it to choose which routers become DR.
example: With other election conditions specified, a priority-255 router is preferred over a lower-priority eligible candidate during a new election.

definition: Injecting routes learnt by one routing protocol into another. Done carelessly in both directions, it can create loops neither protocol can see.
example: Redistributing OSPF into RIP and RIP back into OSPF can make a route circulate for ever.

definition: A link or route repeatedly going down and up, which makes routers keep recomputing and re-advertising. Protocols throttle or dampen to stay stable.
example: A faulty optic that fails every few seconds causes OSPF to rerun SPF again and again.

definition: The network of switches inside a data centre, often a leaf-spine design with many equal-cost paths between any two servers.
example: RFC 7938 describes running BGP on every switch in such a fabric.

definition: Version 4 of the Border Gateway Protocol (RFC 4271), the version used on the Internet today, with extensions such as 32-bit ASNs and IPv6 support.
example: An example Internet border router uses BGP-4 to exchange reachability with a configured neighbour.

definition: Routing between independently run networks (autonomous systems), which on the Internet means BGP. Each network applies its own policy.
example: Your ISP uses inter-domain routing to learn which neighbour can reach a cloud provider's prefixes.

definition: AS numbers reserved for use inside private routing setups and not announced on the Internet: 64512–65534 (16-bit) and 4200000000–4294967294 (32-bit).
example: A data-centre fabric may give every rack switch a private ASN.

definition: A routing design like distance vector, except each route carries the list of networks (in BGP, ASes) it has passed through instead of just a distance. The list lets routers detect loops and apply policy.
example: In BGP the AS_PATH records advertised AS traversal, rather than proving the route followed by data packets.

definition: A BGP attribute recording advertised AS traversal in sequence and other segment forms. Repeated entries can be prepends, and the advertisement is not cryptographic path proof; normal loop checking excludes a route containing the local ASN, subject to explicit exceptions.
example: The advertised AS_SEQUENCE 3356 1299 65010 claims origin 65010 and traversal through 1299 then 3356; it can include prepends or false claims.

definition: The ordinary segment type inside an AS_PATH: an ordered list of ASes. (AS_SET, an unordered type, is deprecated.)
example: In the AS_SEQUENCE 64666 65010, the origin is 65010.

definition: Adding your own ASN to an AS_PATH several times when announcing a route, to make that path look longer and discourage other networks from sending traffic in through it.
example: Announcing 65010 65010 65010 to provider P1 makes paths via P1 look two ASes longer.

definition: The AS claimed to originate a route: the final ASN in an ordinary AS_SEQUENCE path. Origin validation checks whether that claimed origin is authorised for the prefix and length; the path text alone does not prove the actual announcement history.
example: In AS_PATH 3356 1299 65010 the origin AS is 65010.

definition: A router running BGP and exchanging routes with peers.
example: An ISP's border routers are BGP speakers with sessions to customers, peers and providers.

definition: A configured relationship between two BGP speakers, run over TCP port 179, through which they exchange routes.
example: A full mesh of 20 iBGP routers needs 190 BGP sessions.

definition: The first BGP message on a new session, carrying the sender's ASN, proposed hold time, router ID and capabilities.
example: Two routers exchange OPEN messages, then KEEPALIVEs, before any routes.

definition: The BGP message that announces new routes, with their attributes, and withdraws routes that are no longer reachable.
example: When a customer's link fails, its provider sends an UPDATE withdrawing the customer's prefix.

definition: A small BGP message sent periodically to show the session is alive; RFC 4271 suggests sending them at a third of the hold time.
example: For nonzero hold time 90 seconds, RFC 4271’s suggested one-third interval gives KEEPALIVEs no farther apart than 30 seconds.

definition: The BGP message sent when an error is detected; the session is closed straight after it.
example: A fatal session error can cause a NOTIFICATION and closure. Updated BGP error handling can treat some malformed UPDATEs as withdrawals instead.

definition: A BGP session liveness timer, reset by accepted KEEPALIVE or UPDATE messages once established. Negotiated zero disables it; a nonzero proposed hold time must be at least three seconds.
example: With a 90-second hold time, a peer that goes silent is dropped after 90 s.

definition: A BGP extension (RFC 2918) that lets a router ask a peer to resend its routes, for example after changing its import policy.
example: After editing an inbound filter, an operator triggers a route refresh instead of resetting the session.

definition: External BGP: BGP between routers in different ASes, usually over a direct link. Routes sent over eBGP get the sender's ASN prepended to their AS_PATH.
example: An ISP and its customer exchange routes over eBGP.

definition: Internal BGP: BGP between routers in the same AS, used to share externally learnt routes inside the network. Base iBGP does not pass routes learnt from one internal peer to another.
example: An ISP's border routers share Internet routes with each other over iBGP.

definition: A set of nodes in which every pair is directly connected. n nodes need n × (n − 1) / 2 links or sessions.
example: A full mesh of 100 iBGP routers needs 4,950 sessions.

definition: An iBGP router (RFC 4456) allowed to pass routes between its internal clients, so they need sessions only with the reflector instead of a full mesh.
example: With two route reflectors, each of 18 other routers needs just 2 sessions.

definition: BGP attributes added by route reflectors: ORIGINATOR_ID records the router that first injected the route into the AS, and CLUSTER_LIST records reflection clusters passed through, so reflection loops can be detected.
example: A reflector that sees its own cluster ID in CLUSTER_LIST discards the route.

definition: Splitting one AS into sub-ASes that run eBGP-like sessions with each other but look like a single AS to the outside: another way to avoid an iBGP full mesh.
example: A large ISP might split its network into three member ASes inside one confederation.

definition: The properties carried with each BGP route, such as AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, MED and communities, which policies match on and best-path selection compares.
example: A route to 203.0.113.0/24 carries AS_PATH 64500 3356 65010 and NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.1.

definition: The BGP attribute naming the next-hop address for an advertised route. The router must resolve that address through suitable routing state, which can include connected, static or dynamically learned routes.
example: An eBGP route from a peer at 192.0.2.1 normally carries NEXT_HOP 192.0.2.1.

definition: A BGP attribute set inside your own AS and shared over iBGP; higher is preferred. It is checked before AS_PATH length, so it decides which way traffic leaves your network.
example: Give customer routes 300, peer routes 200 and transit routes 100.

definition: Multi-exit discriminator: a BGP attribute a neighbour sets to hint which of several links into it you should use; lower is preferred, and it is normally compared only between routes from the same neighbouring AS.
example: A provider sends MED 10 on its London link and 50 on its Paris link to attract traffic to London.

definition: A tag attached to BGP routes, such as 65010:100, whose meaning is agreed between networks, for example "do not announce to peers" or "prepend towards Europe".
example: In a hypothetical agreed policy, community 65010:100 could request a preference change; the operator must document and honour that convention.

definition: A Cisco-specific BGP value, local to one router and never sent to peers, checked before LOCAL_PREF; higher is preferred.
example: Setting weight 200 on one neighbour makes that router prefer its routes regardless of LOCAL_PREF.

definition: A BGP attribute recording how a route was first introduced: IGP, EGP or incomplete, preferred in that order. Despite the names, it does not prove how the route was learnt.
example: Routes created by a network statement usually carry origin IGP; redistributed ones carry incomplete.

definition: Exterior Gateway Protocol: a historical inter-domain routing protocol preceding BGP. BGP retains EGP as one ORIGIN attribute value; the code alone does not prove a current protocol deployment or how a particular route was learned.
example: BGP’s origin attribute retains an EGP code from the older Exterior Gateway Protocol; the code alone does not prove a live EGP deployment.

definition: The ordered list of tie-breaks a BGP router uses to choose one route per prefix: typically highest LOCAL_PREF, locally originated, shortest AS_PATH, lowest origin, lowest MED, eBGP over iBGP, lowest IGP cost to the next hop, then further tie-breakers. Vendors differ.
example: A route with LOCAL_PREF 300 beats one with 100, however short the second one's AS_PATH.

definition: Choosing an eligible exit with the lowest internal routing cost once earlier BGP selection steps tie. This offloads traffic to another network sooner in the metric sense, not necessarily at the geographically nearest or lowest-latency location.
example: With earlier selection steps tied, a network can choose the exit with lowest IGP cost; that need not minimise geography or elapsed time.

definition: How long a BGP route has been held. Some implementations prefer the oldest of otherwise equal eBGP routes, to avoid needless changes.
example: A documented vendor selection sequence can prefer the older of otherwise tied eBGP paths; configuration can change that step.

definition: Optional BGP behaviour that installs several equally good routes for one prefix for load sharing, instead of only the single best.
example: With multipath on, two equal routes from two transit links can both be used.

definition: A paid service in which a provider carries a customer's traffic to and from the whole Internet.
example: A small ISP buys transit from two large networks for redundancy.

definition: Two networks exchanging traffic directly between their own customers. Settlement-free peering involves no payment for the traffic; paid peering does.
example: Two regional ISPs peer at an exchange so their customers' traffic need not cross a paid transit provider.

definition: A relationship in which a customer buys some agreed transit service from a provider. Simplified commercial-routing models export customer routes widely and peer/provider routes only to customers; contracts, filters and default-only service can differ.
example: A university is a customer of a national research network.

definition: A model of Internet routing policy (Gao and Rexford, 2001): prefer customer routes over peer and provider routes, and export peer and provider routes only to customers. Under its assumptions, BGP converges stably.
example: A network following it never passes a route learnt from one provider to another provider.

definition: The path shape that Gao–Rexford export rules produce: up through providers, across at most one peer link, then down through customers, with no dip from a provider to a customer and back up.
example: Customer → its provider → a peer → that peer's customer is valley-free.

definition: Steering traffic onto chosen paths to balance load, cut cost or improve performance, for example with LOCAL_PREF, prepending, more-specific prefixes or MED.
example: An operator prepends on its expensive link to push inbound traffic onto the cheaper one.

definition: Announcing the same prefix from many locations, so routing delivers each packet to one of them, normally the one routing policy prefers rather than necessarily the closest.
example: A DNS operator can announce the same service prefix from multiple sites; routing policy selects a reachable site without a nearest-site guarantee.

definition: A routing message telling neighbours that a prefix is reachable through the sender, with its attributes.
example: AS 65010 announces 203.0.113.0/24, and its providers pass the announcement on.

definition: A routing advertisement cancelling previously announced reachability. A route may be withdrawn because it became unreachable or because policy changed; withdrawal is not proof of one physical failure.
example: Meta reports that its DNS systems withdrew BGP advertisements after losing data-centre connectivity during the 2021 outage.

definition: An unauthorised announcement for address space, whether accidental or malicious. Accepted more-specific routes can attract traffic ahead of a covering route; filtering, validation and propagation determine the actual impact.
example: In 2008 Pakistan Telecom's /24 hijack drew much of YouTube's traffic away.

definition: Passing routes on to networks that should not receive them under normal export policy, typically re-announcing one provider's or peer's routes to another provider (RFC 7908).
example: In 2019 a small ISP leaked thousands of more-specifics to Verizon, which propagated them.

definition: A product that rewrites or splits BGP routes into more-specifics to steer a network's own traffic. If those routes leak, the more-specifics attract traffic Internet-wide.
example: A BGP optimiser's routes were central to the June 2019 Verizon/DQE leak.

definition: Pakistan Telecommunication Company Limited (AS17557). In February 2008, ordered to block YouTube nationally, it announced a more-specific of YouTube's space that leaked worldwide.
example: Its 208.65.153.0/24 announcement made YouTube unreachable for much of the Internet for about two hours.

definition: A Hong Kong telecoms company whose global network was Pakistan Telecom's upstream in 2008 and propagated the YouTube hijack without filtering it.
example: RIPE RIS saw PCCW withdraw the hijacked route at 21:01 UTC.

definition: RIPE NCC (the European regional Internet registry) runs the Routing Information Service, which collects BGP data from route collectors worldwide. It is a key source for reconstructing incidents.
example: RIS data timed the 2008 YouTube hijack from 18:47 to 21:01 UTC.

definition: Coordinated Universal Time: the world's reference time standard, used to timestamp network events without time-zone confusion.
example: The RIPE incident timeline uses UTC so observers can compare event times without local daylight-saving conventions.

definition: Amazon Web Services' DNS service. In April 2018 attackers hijacked some of its address space via a small ISP and answered DNS queries for MyEtherWallet.
example: Users who clicked through a certificate warning reached a phishing copy of the site.

definition: A web-based cryptocurrency wallet whose DNS was hijacked via BGP in April 2018, sending some users to a phishing site.
example: The attack lasted about two hours.

definition: Tricking people into giving away credentials or money with a fake copy of a trusted site or message.
example: A phishing page looks like a bank's login page but sends the password to the attacker.

definition: A browser error shown when a site's TLS certificate cannot be verified, for example because an impostor is answering for the name.
example: During the 2018 MyEtherWallet hijack, the fake site's certificate did not validate, so browsers warned users.

definition: A large CDN and DNS provider whose engineering blog publishes detailed analyses of Internet routing incidents.
example: Cloudflare documented the 2019 Verizon/DQE leak and the 2021 Facebook outage.

definition: A major US telecoms company. Its AS701 accepted and propagated the leaked routes in the June 2019 DQE incident.
example: Traffic for parts of Cloudflare and Amazon was drawn through a small network via Verizon.

definition: A US network provider whose BGP optimiser generated the more-specific routes that leaked in the June 2019 incident.
example: Its routes reached Verizon through a shared customer, Allegheny Technologies.

definition: On 4 October 2021 a maintenance command disconnected Facebook's (Meta's) backbone; its DNS servers then withdrew their BGP routes, so its names stopped resolving for about six hours.
example: facebook.com, Instagram and WhatsApp all became unreachable.

definition: A DNS server that holds the official records for a domain and answers for it, as opposed to a resolver that looks answers up and caches them.
example: Facebook's own authoritative servers answer for facebook.com.

definition: The high-capacity core network that links an organisation's data centres, sites or regions together.
example: A maintenance command that disconnected the backbone isolated Facebook's data centres from each other.

definition: Resource Public Key Infrastructure: a system of certificates showing which organisation holds which IP prefixes and ASNs, so they can sign ROAs authorising route origins.
example: A network publishes a ROA in RPKI; others' validators check announcements against it.

definition: An RPKI certificate stating that its holder controls certain IP address blocks and AS numbers, issued down a chain from a regional registry's trust anchor.
example: An ISP's resource certificate lists 203.0.112.0/22, so it can sign ROAs for that space.

definition: A starting certificate that validation software is configured to trust; every other certificate is checked by following the chain back to it. Each RIR runs an RPKI trust anchor.
example: A validator follows a valid certificate chain from a configured trust anchor and checks object validity; merely loading anchors does not make every ROA valid.

definition: Route origin authorisation: a signed RPKI object authorising one AS to originate a prefix, with an optional maximum length. Validation checks prefix coverage, origin and length; a ROA alone does not determine route rejection policy.
example: A ROA for 192.0.0.0/22, maxLength 23, AS 65010 allows 65010 to announce the /22 and its /23s.

definition: The greatest prefix length authorised by one ROA record. A longer covered route does not match that record, but another covering validated record may still authorise it and make the route Valid. Allowing lengths you never announce can let forged-origin more-specifics pass origin validation.
example: With maxLength 24 on a /22 you announce only as a /22, an attacker can announce a /24 with your origin and pass.

definition: Software that downloads RPKI objects, checks their signatures back to trust anchors, and gives routers the validated prefix, origin and max-length records to check routes against.
example: A network's routers fetch validated records from two validators for redundancy.

definition: Route origin validation (RFC 6811): classifying each BGP route as Valid, Invalid or NotFound by checking its origin AS and prefix length against validated ROAs. Rejecting Invalid routes is a separate policy choice.
example: If the only covering validated record authorises AS 65010, a covered /24 originated by AS 64666 is Invalid.

definition: Origin validation against validated ROA payloads yields Valid when at least one covering record authorises both origin and length, Invalid when covering records exist but none authorises both, and NotFound when no validated record covers the route.
example: With no covering validated record, the hypothetical announcement is NotFound rather than Invalid.

definition: A BGP extension that cryptographically protects AS-path propagation among participating BGPsec speakers. A fully protected path needs the required signatures and validation; it does not sign every forwarded data packet or establish universal deployment.
example: A forged AS-path claim lacks the necessary valid BGPsec signatures under a fully protected participating path; handling mixed deployments needs the protocol rules.

definition: Autonomous system provider authorisation: RPKI relationship data identifying an AS’s authorised providers. Validation procedures can detect particular path-policy violations using that data; specification status and coverage must be checked against the dated IETF documents.
example: If AS 65010 lists only providers 3356 and 1299, a path showing 65010 behind 64666 looks suspicious.

definition: Accepting from a neighbour only the routes it is entitled to announce, for example only a customer's registered prefixes, and capping how many it may send.
example: A provider that filters a customer to 203.0.112.0/22 would reject a hijacked YouTube /24 from it.

aliases: Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security
definition: Mutually Agreed Norms for Routing Security: an industry initiative setting baseline routing-security actions, such as filtering customers' announcements and publishing routing data.
example: An ISP joining MANRS commits to filter routes from its customers.

definition: The IPv4 address 0.0.0.0 used as a source address to mean "I have no address yet". (In a route, 0.0.0.0/0 instead means every address.)
example: A DHCP Discover is sent from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255.

definition: The usual four-message DHCPv4 exchange: Discover (client looks for servers), Offer (a server proposes an address), Request (client picks one offer) and Ack (that server confirms).
example: A laptop runs DORA and ends up with 192.168.1.42/24 for 24 hours.

definition: The first DHCP message: the client broadcasts it from 0.0.0.0 to find servers.
example: Discover goes from UDP port 68 to port 67 as a limited broadcast.

definition: A DHCP server's reply to Discover, offering an address and settings. Several servers may offer.
example: A server offers 192.168.1.42 with a 24-hour lease.

definition: The client message accepting one server's offer (broadcast, naming that server in option 54), and later used to renew or rebind a lease.
example: Broadcasting it lets other servers see their offers were declined.

definition: The DHCP server's confirmation that the client may use the address, with the lease time and options.
example: After the DHCPACK, the client ARP-probes the address before using it.

definition: A DHCP server's refusal of a client's request, for example for an address on the wrong subnet. The client restarts from Discover.
example: A laptop moved to a new VLAN asks for its old address and gets a DHCPNAK.

definition: The message a DHCP client sends when the offered address turns out to be in use already; it then restarts after a delay.
example: An ARP probe gets an answer, so the client declines the address.

definition: The optional message a DHCP client sends to give its address back early when leaving the network.
example: A laptop shutting down cleanly may release its lease.

definition: A random 32-bit number a DHCP client puts in its messages so it can match replies to its own requests.
example: Two clients discovering at once tell their replies apart by xid.

definition: The DHCP option carrying the chosen server's address. The client includes it in its Request to say which offer it accepts.
example: Option 54 = 192.168.1.1 tells every server that 192.168.1.1's offer was chosen.

definition: DHCPv4 options carry configuration and message metadata. Most use type-length-value encoding; Pad and End are single-byte exceptions. Common codes include subnet mask 1, router 3, DNS 6, requested address 50, lease 51 and message type 53.
example: Option 55 lists the options a client wants, such as 1, 3 and 6.

definition: An encoding where each field is a type code, a length, then that many bytes of value, so a parser can skip fields it does not understand.
example: Bytes 51, 4, 0, 0, 14, 16 are option 51 with 4 bytes of value: a 3,600-second lease.

definition: Special one-byte DHCP options with no length: Pad (code 0) fills space and End (code 255) marks the end of the options.
example: A parser skips 0 bytes and stops at 255.

definition: Bootstrap Protocol: DHCP's predecessor. DHCPv4 still uses its message format, ports 67 and 68, and field names such as yiaddr and giaddr.
example: A DHCP message is a BOOTP message with a magic cookie and DHCP options added.

definition: The four-byte value 99, 130, 83, 99 identifying the RFC 1048-style vendor/options area used by DHCPv4. BOOTP also supports this cookie, so the cookie alone does not distinguish DHCP from every BOOTP message.
example: A parser checks for the magic cookie before reading options.

definition: A DHCP option (52) that lets options spill into the BOOTP file and server-name fields when the normal options area is full.
example: A server with very long options may set option overload.

definition: DHCP header fields: ciaddr is the client's current address, yiaddr the address offered to it ("your"), giaddr the relay agent's address, and chaddr the client hardware (MAC) address.
example: An Offer carries yiaddr 192.168.1.42 and the client's MAC in chaddr.

definition: The DHCP field a relay agent fills with the address of the interface the client's broadcast arrived on. The server uses it to choose the right address pool and sends its reply back to that address.
example: A relay on VLAN 20 sets giaddr 10.20.0.1, so the server offers from 10.20.0.0/24.

definition: Permission to use an address for a specified lease duration; DHCP also represents an infinite lease. With a finite lease, the client must obtain renewed permission or stop using the address when it expires.
example: Ignoring overrides and variation, a 24-hour lease beginning at midnight reaches nominal T1 at noon and expires at midnight if not renewed.

definition: DHCP client timers measured from the start of a lease. At T1 (by default 50% of the lease) the client starts renewing with its server; at T2 (87.5%) it starts rebinding with any server.
example: For an 8-hour lease starting at 09:00, exact nominal default fractions give T1 at 13:00 and T2 at 16:00.

definition: The DHCP phase starting at T2 when a client that could not renew with its own server broadcasts a Request so any server with the lease information can extend it.
example: With exact default fractions for a midnight 24-hour lease, an authorised state-sharing server may answer the T2 broadcast at 21:00.

definition: The DHCP phase from T1 when the client unicasts a Request to the server that granted its lease, asking to extend it.
example: A midnight 24-hour lease reaches nominal default T1 at noon; client policy and server options can alter actual renewal timing.

definition: A server configuration associating an intended stable address with a particular client identifier, often a MAC address or DHCP client identifier. Identity changes, conflicts and server policy can prevent the expected assignment.
example: A printer gets a reservation so it is always 192.168.1.50.

definition: A value (DHCP option 61) a client sends to identify itself to the server, used instead of or as well as its MAC.
example: A reservation can survive a network-card change if the client presents the same configured identifier and the server uses it as intended.

definition: Devices using a random MAC address instead of their hardware one, often per network, to make tracking harder. It can break MAC-based DHCP reservations.
example: A client can use a per-network or rotating MAC according to its platform configuration; it need not choose a fresh value on every join.

definition: A router function that receives DHCP broadcasts on a local subnet and forwards them as unicast to a central DHCP server, filling in giaddr, then passes the replies back.
example: Cisco's ip helper-address makes a router interface a DHCP relay.

definition: A DHCP option a relay agent adds to say which switch port or circuit a request came from (RFC 3046). ISPs use it to tie addresses to physical lines.
example: A server gives a fixed address to whichever device is on a given customer's line.

definition: Virtual LAN: a logical layer-two broadcast domain configured on switching infrastructure. Tags identify VLANs on tagged links; access frames can be untagged, and a VLAN does not inherently require exactly one IP subnet.
example: Staff on VLAN 10 and guests on VLAN 20 share switches but not broadcasts.

definition: Local area network: a network covering one building or site, such as a home or office, typically Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
example: Your laptop and printer at home are on the same LAN.

definition: Wide area network: links spanning long distances; on a home router, the WAN side faces the ISP.
example: A home router has a LAN side 192.168.1.1 and a WAN side 203.0.113.7.

definition: A device that forwards Ethernet frames between its ports by MAC address within a LAN. Managed switches add features such as VLANs and DHCP snooping.
example: An office switch connects 48 desks and an uplink to the router.

definition: An IPv4 Address Conflict Detection ARP request with sender protocol address 0.0.0.0 and the candidate address as target. An ARP Announcement is a different packet that announces the claimed address after probing.
example: RFC 5227 uses a sequence of probes before claiming an address. No observed conflict is not an absolute uniqueness guarantee.

definition: An unsolicited ARP message about the sender’s own IPv4 address, often used to announce a mapping. RFC 5227 ARP Announcements are a specified request form; receivers and policy determine whether caches are updated.
example: After a failover, the new server sends a gratuitous ARP so neighbours send to its MAC.

definition: An unauthorised DHCP server on a network, malicious or accidental, handing out wrong settings such as its own address as gateway or DNS.
example: Someone plugs in a home router with DHCP on, and new clients get 192.168.0.x addresses.

definition: A managed-switch feature that drops DHCP server messages arriving on untrusted ports and records which address each port's client was given.
example: With only the uplink trusted, a rogue server on a desk port is ignored.

definition: In DHCP snooping, a trusted ingress port is allowed to carry server-originated DHCP messages. An untrusted ingress port is subject to server-message restrictions; a compromised trusted server still needs separate protection.
example: Mark the uplink trusted and every desk port untrusted.

definition: The table a DHCP-snooping switch builds of MAC address, IP address, port and VLAN from the leases it sees, used by ARP inspection and source guard.
example: An entry might read 3c:22:fb:12:34:56, 10.20.0.57, port 12, VLAN 20.

definition: Dynamic ARP inspection: a switch feature that drops ARP messages whose IP-to-MAC claims do not match the snooping binding table or configured exceptions, blocking ARP spoofing.
example: A host claiming to be the gateway in forged ARP replies has them dropped.

definition: A switch feature that drops packets from an access port unless their source address (and optionally MAC) matches the binding for that port.
example: A host trying to send with someone else's IP is blocked at its switch port.

definition: Access control list: a list of rules permitting or denying traffic by fields such as addresses and ports, applied on an interface or in a feature.
example: An ACL can allow ARP from a static server whose address is not in the snooping table.

definition: A position or attack in which an intermediary relays, redirects or alters communication between parties. Whether it can read application plaintext depends on encryption and authentication; forwarding traffic through an attacker alone does not defeat properly authenticated TLS.
example: A rogue DHCP server naming itself as gateway puts itself in the middle of clients' off-link traffic.

definition: Optional authentication mechanisms for DHCP messages, including RFC 3118. Without effective authentication or network-access controls, base DHCPv4 does not let a client establish server identity merely from a received Offer.
example: A managed network can enforce DHCP snooping trust boundaries; that protects a different boundary from cryptographic message authentication.

definition: A DHCP option allowing a two-message exchange (Discover/Ack in DHCPv4, Solicit/Reply in DHCPv6) instead of four.
example: A client and server that both support Rapid Commit skip the Offer and Request.

definition: The usual four DHCPv6 messages, the IPv6 counterpart of DHCPv4's DORA. Clients send to a link-local multicast address rather than a broadcast.
example: A home router solicits a prefix from its ISP and receives it in the Reply.

definition: A DHCPv6 feature that gives a requesting router a whole IPv6 prefix, such as a /56 or /48, to divide into /64 subnets for its own networks.
example: An ISP delegates 2001:db8:ab00::/56 to a home router, which can make 256 /64s.

definition: A DNS server that looks up names on behalf of clients, querying authoritative servers and caching the answers.
example: A home router's resolver forwards your query to the ISP's resolvers.

definition: TCP’s SYN flag synchronises initial sequence numbers; ordinary connection establishment uses SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK segments. SYN-bearing segments may carry options such as MSS, but a SYN is not a guarantee that the MSS option is present.
example: A browser's SYN to 198.51.100.80:443 starts the TCP handshake.

definition: The SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK exchange that opens a TCP connection. It uses small packets, so it can succeed even when full-size packets are being lost.
example: A PMTUD black hole lets the handshake complete but stalls the first big data packets.

definition: A router at the edge of a network that connects it to other networks, typically running BGP with neighbours.
example: An ISP's border router learns the server's /24 from a hosting provider over BGP.

definition: One thousandth of a second. Network delays are usually quoted in milliseconds.
example: A traceroute hop at 15 ms means a round trip of 0.015 seconds.

definition: Megabits per second: millions of bits per second, a unit of link speed. 1,000 Mbit/s is 1 Gbit/s.
example: A 100 Mbit/s link carries at most 12.5 megabytes per second.

definition: Gigabits per second: thousands of millions (10 to the power 9) of bits per second.
example: 1 Gbit/s is 125,000,000 bytes per second.

definition: Kilobyte is the decimal multiple of 1,000 bytes. KiB means 1,024 bytes; some older texts use KB ambiguously, so an example should state its exact byte count.
example: The fragmentation example uses exactly 8,192 bytes, which is 8 KiB; calling it 8 KB without a definition would be ambiguous.

definition: In OSPF and IS-IS, shortest path first: each router running Dijkstra's algorithm over its link-state database to compute routes, with itself as the root. (In email, SPF instead means Sender Policy Framework, a DNS record listing which servers may send a domain's mail.)
example: After relevant LSDB changes, routers schedule the needed path calculations; batching and incremental algorithms avoid a guarantee of one full run per event.

definition: Recording observed network packets for inspection with tools such as tcpdump or Wireshark. Capture location, offloading, filtering and encryption limit what the trace establishes.
example: A capture on the WAN link shows SYNs leaving but no SYN-ACKs returning.

definition: Sending successive packets or requests to each path or server in turn. Per-packet round-robin balances packet counts but can reorder a flow's packets across paths of different delay.
example: Packets 1, 2, 3, 4 go out of links A, B, C, D, then packet 5 out of A again.

definition: A transport protocol retransmitting or slowing down because it wrongly concluded a packet was lost, for example when packets were merely reordered.
example: Three packets overtaking an earlier one can trigger TCP fast retransmit even though nothing was lost.

definition: Being connected to more than one network or having several addresses, such as a host with two interfaces or a site with two ISPs. Replies may come from a different address than expected.
example: A multi-homed server might answer a traceroute from its second interface.

definition: In a TCAM entry, the bits that must match exactly; the remaining bits are don't-care. A prefix's network bits are its fixed bits.
example: 10.1.0.0/16 has 16 fixed bits and 16 don't-care bits.

definition: Traffic spread unevenly across paths that should share it, for example when flow hashing puts several large flows on one link.
example: Two elephant flows on one of four links leave it congested while the others are half empty.

definition: In Happy Eyeballs, how long a client waits for one connection attempt before starting the next in parallel. RFC 8305 recommends 250 ms by default.
example: IPv6 is tried first; if it has not connected after 250 ms, an IPv4 attempt starts alongside it.

definition: A host, interface or network providing IPv6 service without native IPv4 service in the relevant context. Translation such as NAT64 or application proxies can still provide access to some IPv4 destinations; IPv4-dependent applications may need additional support.
example: Some mobile operators run IPv6-only networks with NAT64 and 464XLAT.

definition: BGP: the routing protocol (BGP-4, RFC 4271) that autonomous systems use to exchange reachability and apply routing policy between each other. It runs over TCP port 179 and chooses paths by policy rather than speed.
example: Your ISP learns, over BGP, that a cloud provider's prefix is reachable through a particular neighbour.

definition: DHCP: the protocol a device uses on joining a network to get an IP address, subnet mask, default gateway, DNS servers and a lease time from a server.
example: A laptop joining café Wi-Fi gets 192.168.1.42/24 and gateway 192.168.1.1 by DHCP.

definition: In IPv6, RA means Router Advertisement, an ICMPv6 message with router lifetime, flags and optional configuration. The DNS-header RA bit instead means Recursion Available; these are different protocol meanings.
example: The M flag indicates managed address configuration is available; client support and the separate prefix A flag affect how the host configures itself.

definition: An election in which a newly arriving higher-ranked candidate does not automatically replace an existing winner. OSPF’s DR election follows this rule; failures, interface changes and administrative restarts can still trigger a change.
example: A newly arriving priority-255 router does not pre-empt an existing DR solely because its priority is higher.

definition: In networking, the whole range of possible addresses, or a block of it held by an organisation. IPv4 has 2 to the power 32 values; IPv6 has 2 to the power 128.
example: Overlapping private address space at two merged sites makes 10.0.5.20 ambiguous.

definition: A single link, such as an Ethernet LAN, that several routers attach to, so each can reach all the others directly. OSPF elects a designated router on such a segment to avoid every pair forming a full adjacency.
example: Ten OSPF routers plugged into one switch VLAN share one segment: with a DR and BDR they form 17 full adjacencies instead of 45.

definition: A router or managed cloud service that performs network address translation for a private network, letting its hosts start connections to the Internet through one or a few public addresses.
example: Servers in a cloud provider's private subnet reach software updates through the provider's NAT gateway.

definition: The route followed by a response towards the original sender. It can differ from the forward route; round-trip timing includes both directions and does not isolate a single link’s delay.
Zero bytes used to make the complete IPv4 header length a multiple of four bytes after its options. It is different from Ethernet frame padding used to reach a link-layer minimum frame size.
Python ipaddress network parsing that rejects an address with nonzero host bits for its supplied prefix. IPv4Interface instead represents an interface address and its associated network.

Methods that let applications communicate across NAT mapping and filtering, including observed-address discovery, connectivity checks, mapping control and relays. STUN, ICE and TURN have different roles; none guarantees that every topology has a usable direct path.

The routing metric assigned to one link or outgoing interface. A shortest-path routing model adds those costs along a path; RIP normally uses one per network, while OSPF uses configured interface costs. This is distinct from the accumulated spanning-tree cost to a root bridge.
